title: Agent-as-a-Judge: Evaluate Agents with Agents
author: Mingchen Zhuge · Changsheng Zhao · Dylan R. Ashley · Wenyi Wang · Dmitrii Khizbullin · Yunyang Xiong · Zechun Liu · Ernie Chang · Raghuraman Krishnamoorthi · Yuandong Tian · Yangyang Shi · Vikas Chandra · Jürgen Schmidhuber

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Benchmark governance: High scores may lack workplace meaning
st.an: The supplied material consists only of bibliographic references to agent benchmarks, model-based judging and related systems. It provides no substantive claims, methods or results from Agent-as-a-Judge showing whether benchmark scores translate into reliable workplace performance, or addressing benchmark governance, reproducibility, incentives or lifecycle assurance.

st.t: Professional evaluation: Realistic tasks complicate reproducible scoring
st.an: The excerpts provide relevant context on tool-using agents and LLM-based judging, but they do not directly endorse the cluster’s central claim that credible evaluation must test realistic professional task execution, nor do they establish how automated judging should be separately validated. Reported claims are attributed to prior work rather than demonstrated by this source.
qs: LLM-as-a-Judge In the domain of AI evaluation and judgment, frameworks (Zheng et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2023) have pioneered the use of LLMs to assess conversational agents, demonstrating how LLMs can evaluate dialogue quality and consistency.
However, the challenge of maintaining coherence in agents’ dialogue and preventing hallucination remains prominent (Du et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2023c).

st.t: Agent benchmarks: Protocol scores are not competence
st.an: The source accepts that existing code benchmarks inadequately reflect practical agent performance and materially extends the cluster by proposing agentic judges that provide intermediate feedback at lower claimed cost. However, it does not quantitatively validate the judge, so it supports the framework’s promise rather than establishing its reliability.
qs: Although they are useful for evaluating the basic skills of foundation models, neither of these two reflects the most practical challenges developers face.

It not only retains the cost-effectiveness of LLM-as-a-Judge but is also equipped with agentic features, allowing it to provide rich intermediate feedback throughout the entire process, as it acts as an agentic system.

st.t: Evaluation design: Preferences differ from professional correctness
st.an: The source accepts that simple correctness benchmarks do not capture realistic professional workflows and concretely extends evaluation toward nuanced, agent-based judgment across domains. This develops the cluster’s measurement-design proposition, although the supplied excerpts provide aims and related-work discussion rather than results validating the proposed evaluator.
qs: While these benchmarks are useful for evaluating the correctness of generated code, they are limited in complexity and do not fully represent the challenges encountered in real-world software development.
Our work builds on these advancements by exploring how LLMs can perform more nuanced judgment tasks, further investigating their potential in decision-making across various domains.

st.t: Evaluation validity: Benchmark safeguards impose trade-offs
st.an: The source accepts the need for stronger agent evaluation and materially develops it by proposing end-to-end, process-aware benchmarks that expose intermediate failures and provide richer signals than final-outcome scores. It also adds evaluation-efficiency as a design criterion, while offering methodological proposals rather than demonstrated performance or labour-saving results.
qs: Moreover, none of them accurately reflect the intermediate stages of development or provide sufficient reward signals for long-horizon development—similar issues are present in OpenAI’s recent MLE-Bench (Chan et al., 2024).
Second, it should emphasize the development process, not just final outcomes (e.g., pass@1 rates offer limited feedback and fail to highlight intermediate problems).

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source extends the synthesis with non-legal developer-agent evidence showing low complete-task performance, substantial intermediate failures, and evaluation results that depend on task context and a fallible human-consensus reference. This materially reinforces the cluster’s claims that agentic capability remains jagged and that evaluation must be task-specific rather than treated as proof of general competence.

st.t: Legal benchmarks: Realistic tasks expose uneven competence
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central methodological proposition by arguing, in the coding context, that simple correctness benchmarks lack real-world representativeness and that evaluation should move toward more complex, realistic tasks. It does not provide legal-domain evidence or empirical results on uneven legal competence, sourcing failures, or grading reliability.
qs: While these benchmarks are useful for evaluating the correctness of generated code, they are limited in complexity and do not fully represent the challenges encountered in real-world software development.
As the field progressed, newer benchmarks began to focus on more complex and realistic tasks.

kp.k: Agentic evaluation addresses weaknesses in outcome-only assessment
kp.d: The authors propose Agent-as-a-Judge as an extension of LLM-as-a-Judge for evaluating multistep agentic systems. Their argument is that final-outcome metrics obscure intermediate failures, while detailed human assessment is expensive. The paper provides cross-domain evidence from automated AI development, not direct evidence about legal services.
qs: We instead propose that agentic systems should be used to evaluate agentic systems.

It not only retains the cost-effectiveness of LLM-as-a-Judge but is also equipped with agentic features, allowing it to provide rich intermediate feedback throughout the entire process, as it acts as an agentic system.

kp.k: Existing coding benchmarks risk narrowness and benchmark targeting
kp.d: The authors argue that algorithmic and software-repair benchmarks cover only parts of development and inadequately assess intermediate stages. They report prior research showing that LLMs can solve over 27% of SWE-Bench tasks without advanced agentic systems, and criticise task-specific mechanisms as risking poor real-world generalisation. These are reported findings and methodological arguments, rather than results of their DevAI experiments.
qs: HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), for example, focuses exclusively on algorithmic problems, while MBPP (Austin et al., 2021) deals with simple programming tasks.
Concerningly, recent research shows that large language models (LLMs) can already solve over 27% of the tasks in SWE-Bench without needing of advanced agentic systems (Xia et al., 2024).

kp.k: DevAI evaluates development through hierarchical requirements
kp.d: DevAI contains 55 curated AI development tasks, 365 requirements and 125 optional preferences. Requirements have dependencies represented as a directed acyclic graph, enabling assessment of intermediate milestones rather than only complete-task success. Tasks are relatively small-scale and computationally inexpensive, covering areas including supervised learning, reinforcement learning, computer vision and natural language processing. The authors distinguish binary requirements from softer preferences and prioritise development processes rather than model-performance scores.
qs: DevAI consists of a curated set of 55 tasks, each defined by (1) a plain text user query that describes an AI development task; (2) a set of plain text requirements (for a total of 365 requirements), each with a set of dependencies connecting them to other requirements; and (3) a set of preferences (for a total of 125 preferences) which represent softer requirements.
This allows for more comprehensive non-sparse feedback than a binary success metric.
Importantly, to avoid ambiguity, we set the requirements to be explicit, binary, and straightforward to evaluate.

kp.k: Developer agents rarely completed entire benchmark tasks
kp.d: The study tested MetaGPT Data Interpreter, GPT-Pilot 0.2.13 and OpenHands CodeAct v1.9 using gpt-4o-2024-05-13, with an 1800-second limit per task. Human consensus found independent requirement satisfaction of 22.13%, 44.80% and 42.89%, respectively; accounting for dependencies reduced these figures to 6.55%, 28.96% and 28.68%. Complete-task solve rates were 0.00%, 1.81% and 1.81%. These results concern the tested configurations and constrained DevAI tasks, not unrestricted software-development capability.
qs: These AI developers were given a time-limit of 1800 seconds to solve each task and were forcefully halted if they exceeded this time limit

We found that the two best- performing methods (GPT-Pilot and OpenHands) could satisfy about 29% of the requirements (or around 44% if prerequisites are ignored) but only on one task could they meet all the requirements.

kp.k: Operational efficiency varied independently of task success
kp.d: Table 1 reports average development costs of $1.19 for MetaGPT, $3.92 for GPT-Pilot and $6.38 for OpenHands, with average times of 775.29s, 1622.38s and 362.41s. GPT-Pilot generated the most saved code files and lines, while MetaGPT saved relatively little code. The authors explicitly caution that these operational statistics do not directly indicate performance.
qs: On average, a full evaluation on DevAI with one of these three took around 210.65 USD and 14 hours to perform.
Note that the results in Table 1 are not directly indicative of performance but provide valuable insights into the practical utility of DevAI and the performance of AI developers.

kp.k: Human evaluation exhibited substantial disagreement and ambiguity
kp.d: Three AI experts recruited from the authors initially assessed outputs with minimal instructions, spending 58 human hours. Pairwise disagreement ranged from around 10% to 30%, reflecting missed evidence and differing interpretations. A subsequent 9.5-hour joint discussion added 28.5 person-hours and produced the consensus baseline. The authors explicitly acknowledge that consensus is an approximation rather than absolute ground truth.
qs: We recruited three AI experts from the authors to perform human evaluation on the output of agentic code generation systems.
The results indicate that the disagreement rates between pairs of evaluators range from around 10% to 30%.
Additionally, some disagreements are not necessarily incorrect but arise from differing perspectives on how ambiguity should be resolved.

While the consensus evaluation may not represent the absolute ground truth (we acknowledge that some quantity of error likely would still exist even after this procedure), we expect the consensus evaluation to more accurately approximate any extant ground truth (Clemen, 1989).

kp.k: Debate and aggregation can improve human assessment
kp.d: The authors recommend evidence-based debate after individual judgments or a larger expert panel using majority voting. Majority voting more closely matched consensus than individual assessments, although it retained errors. They favour debate when recruiting additional experts is costly or impractical; their recommendations depend on assumptions about the reliability of consensus and individual evaluators.
qs: First, like in this work, introduce a debate round after each judgment, where individuals present evidence and either persuade others or adjust their own opinions after discussion.
As seen in the results, although significant errors occur among all evaluators, the majority vote effectively corrects most of these errors.

kp.k: Tool-supported evidence gathering improves automated judgments
kp.d: The proof of concept initially comprised graph, locate, read, search, retrieve, ask, memory and planning modules. These inspect project structure, identify relevant files, read multimodal artifacts and retrieve execution feedback before judging individual requirements. The read module supports 33 formats. Ablations favoured a reduced combination of graph, locate, read, retrieve and ask, rather than the full initial architecture.
qs: After conducting comprehensive ablation studies, we found that the modular combination of (1), (2), (3), (5), and (6) achieved the highest performance (see Appendix K).

kp.k: Agent judges outperform LLM judges against human consensus
kp.d: Table 3 reports black-box alignment for Agent-as-a-Judge of 88.52%, 83.88% and 90.44% for MetaGPT, GPT-Pilot and OpenHands, versus 84.15%, 65.30% and 60.38% for LLM-as-a-Judge. With manually collected trajectories in gray-box settings, agent alignment was 92.07%, 86.61% and 90.16%, versus 68.86%, 71.85% and 70.76%. Gray-box agent scores exceeded average individual-human alignment for all three developers, but human majority voting remained higher at 95.08%, 93.98% and 94.26%. Thus, agreement with consensus supports the proof of concept without demonstrating universal superiority over expert panels.
qs: It is defined as the percentage of requirement evaluations that are the same as the Human-as-a-Judge consensus evaluation.
Compared to LLM-as-a-Judge, Agent- as-a-Judge consistently achieves a higher Alignment Rate, closely matching human judgments.

kp.k: Class imbalance complicates interpretation of judge accuracy
kp.d: The authors warn that requirement failures are more common than successes, so aggregate alignment and judge-shift metrics can be misleading. They use precision–recall curves to assess performance more meaningfully and report that the agent judge outperformed individual evaluators for OpenHands in that analysis. This is a task-specific comparison, not evidence that agent judges can replace humans generally.
qs: Metrics like judge shift and alignment rate can be misleading.
For example, since MetaGPT rarely meets requirements, LLM-as-a-Judge easily identifies most cases as negative (achieving 84.15% in the black-box setting).
Agent-as-a-Judge even outperforms any single human evaluator on OpenHands and aligns closest with majority voting.

kp.k: Additional agent complexity can reduce evaluation reliability
kp.d: For OpenHands, adding graph, read and locate to ask increased alignment from 65.03% to 75.95%, 82.24% and 90.44%; adding retrieve yielded 90.16%. Appendix K reports lower alignment with search, planning and memory. The authors hypothesise that noisy retrieval, unstable planning and carry-over bias from earlier judgments explain these declines. Their alternative-search experiments also suggest that the small workspaces limited search's usefulness.
qs: When planning is unstable, the evidence collected from different actions can become inconsistent, leading to a decline in performance.
Finally, we experimented with a memory mechanism.
However, in practice, we saw no improvement.

We suspect that the interconnected nature of the requirements may have caused biases: specifically, once a prior requirement was fulfilled, it might have overly influenced positive judgments on subsequent requirements, even if they were not fully met.

kp.k: Trajectory access helps selectively, not uniformly
kp.d: Gray-box evaluation uses carefully collected execution trajectories, whereas black-box evaluation does not require them. Retrieval improved GPT-Pilot alignment from 83.88% to 86.61%, but slightly reduced OpenHands alignment from 90.44% to 90.16%. Appendix K reports that removing the beginning of long trajectories and the middle of individual steps worked best in the GPT-Pilot truncation experiments. The paper presents access to suitable trajectory data as a practical constraint.
qs: In contrast, as shown in Table 3, the judgment of MetaGPT and GPT-Pilot indicates that retrieve is useful, as the trajectory provides additional valuable information.
By focusing on these retrieval strategies, we can significantly enhance the per- formance of the retrieve component, particularly in complex scenarios like GPT-Pilot.

kp.k: Automated evaluation sharply reduces estimated human evaluation costs
kp.d: The study reports 86.5 person-hours for human evaluation, valued at $1297.50 using an assumed $15 hourly wage for AI subject experts. Agent-as-a-Judge required $30.58 in API calls and 118.43 minutes; LLM-as-a-Judge required $29.63 and 10.99 minutes. The introduction reports savings of 97.72% in time and 97.64% in cost. Section 4.4 separately labels the agent's shares as 2.29% of cost and 2.36% of time; the document's percentage descriptions are not consistent, so the absolute reported quantities are retained here.
qs: The Human-as-a-Judge took the three evaluators a self-reported total of 86.5 hours.
With a 15 USD minimum wage (assuming this would buy a subject expert in AI), a full evaluation under DevAI would cost around 1297.50 USD.
LLM-as-a-Judge was faster at 10.99 minutes, but due to the absence of intelligent context selection by the Agent-as-a-Judge’s modules, it still cost 29.63 USD.

kp.k: Self-improvement through intermediate feedback remains a proposed direction
kp.d: The authors propose using requirement-level feedback for on-the-fly correction, process-supervised reward models and mutual improvement between developers and judges. They hypothesise an agentic self-play cycle whose successive improvements reinforce one another and may help embed agentic capabilities into foundation models. These are prospective mechanisms, explicitly not fully exploited by the reported evaluation experiments.
qs: A key power of the Agent-as-a-Judge, though not fully exploited here but nonetheless clear, is that it provides intermediate feedback that is essential for effective and efficient optimization (Zhuge et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2024).
By introducing Agent-as-a-Judge, we create the opportunity to build a process-supervised reward model (PRM) for improving agentic systems (Lightman et al., 2023).
The cycle of mutual improvement between the Agent-as-a-Judge and the evaluated agents, where both evolve together through iterative feedback, presents a promising direction.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Zhuge and coauthors claim that agentic evaluators can reduce the human effort required to evaluate AI development agents while providing richer feedback and better agreement with human consensus than LLM-only evaluators.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about automated AI development, not legal services or judicial decision-making. The authors present Agent-as-a-Judge as an extension of LLM-as-a-Judge that inspects project files, artifacts and, where available, execution trajectories to assess individual requirements. Their proof-of-concept supports a claim of performance comparable to human evaluators and possible substitution for individual evaluators in some settings. They also report substantial remaining limitations in the developer agents themselves: GPT-Pilot and OpenHands each satisfied approximately 29% of requirements when dependencies were counted and completed only one full task each. Separately, the authors predict that intermediate evaluative feedback could enable agents to correct problems during development, support process-supervised reward models and create a cycle of mutual improvement between developers and evaluators. These self-improvement claims are presented as future possibilities rather than demonstrated outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of the authors’ DevAI benchmark, comparisons against three author-experts’ consensus assessments, component ablations and an evaluation-cost calculation.
pts.d: DevAI contains 55 AI development tasks, 365 hierarchical requirements and 125 optional preferences. The authors tested MetaGPT, GPT-Pilot and OpenHands. Table 3 reports Agent-as-a-Judge agreement with human consensus of 83.88%–90.44% without collected trajectories and 86.61%–92.07% with trajectories, compared with 60.38%–84.15% and 68.86%–71.85%, respectively, for LLM-as-a-Judge. Individual human averages were 84.88%–89.34%; majority-vote agreement was 93.98%–95.08%. Human consensus followed an initial assessment round and a discussion round. The authors acknowledge that consensus is not absolute ground truth and that aggregate alignment and judge-shift metrics can be misleading; they also use precision-recall curves. The cost comparison reports 86.5 self-reported human hours, valued at $1,297.50 using an assumed $15 hourly expert wage, versus $30.58 in API calls and 118.43 minutes for Agent-as-a-Judge. Percentage summaries differ within the paper, so the underlying totals are preserved here. Ablations show gains from graph, read and locate components, but no consistent benefit from adding search, planning or memory in these workspaces. The prospective self-improvement cycle is supported by conceptual argument and related research, not a demonstrated iterative training experiment.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The measured claims concern an October 2024 proof-of-concept under constrained benchmark conditions; broader self-improvement predictions have no specified delivery date.
pts.d: The developer agents used gpt-4o-2024-05-13 and had 1,800 seconds per task, including execution, with no guaranteed GPU. Tasks were deliberately small-scale and relatively inexpensive to run. Evaluation requirements were intended to be explicit and binary, while subjective preferences were separated out. Gray-box evaluation depends on carefully collected trajectories that the authors describe as difficult to obtain in practice; black-box evaluation does not require those trajectories. The authors qualify replacement of human evaluators as possible in some cases, not universal. They acknowledge remaining uncertainty in the human-consensus reference and describe intermediate-feedback optimization as not fully exploited in this study. Predictions about self-play, mutually improving agents and greater benefits from search in larger workspaces are conditional outlooks rather than time-bound forecasts.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The identified beneficiaries are AI researchers, developer-agent builders and organizations conducting expert evaluation; some expert evaluation work could be automated.
pts.d: The authors envisage reducing expert labor and evaluation expenditure, enabling developers to obtain detailed requirement-level feedback at greater scale, and helping agent builders identify failures hidden by final task-success measures. Research engineers and users of AI development systems are also affected by the limited end-to-end task completion observed and by workflow problems described in the authors’ qualitative experience, including skipped code execution and manual intervention. The proposed substitution concerns evaluation of software-development outputs, not replacement of software engineers generally. The paper provides no claims or evidence about lawyers, law firms, legal clients, legal markets or human verification of legal advice.
